basis: New mission, no workbook source; written per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, angle distinct from sdg4-1 (STEM/exam pressure) and sdg4-2 (digital equity/media literacy): the status and outcomes of vocational/technical education specifically. Facts and sources: vocational-school enrollment share fell from 59.6% (98th academic year) to 46.68% (112th academic year), a 16-year low; ratio was 7:3 forty-plus years ago; academic track overtook vocational in the 108th academic year; by the 113th academic year, general-track students ~279,000 (down 11,000) vs vocational students ~210,000 (down 52,000) (udn.com, CNA reporting Ministry of Education statistics, 2024-2025). Stigma ('black hands'/blue-collar label vs 'craftsman'/'technician' respect elsewhere) and parental credential-insistence even alongside direct-to-job tracks (Global Views Monthly, Liberty Times, CNA, 2024-2025). WorldSkills 2024 (47th, Lyon): Taiwan 58 competitors/50 trades, 2 gold/3 silver/10 bronze/28 excellence, 4th of 69 countries (Ministry of Labor press release Sep 2024, via udn.com/TBO Taiwan). WorldSkills Asia 2025 (Taipei, hosted by Taiwan): back-to-back overall team champion, 17 gold/9 silver/5 bronze/2 excellence youth + 5 gold junior, among 30 countries (Ministry of Labor 2025). Dual-Track Training Flagship Program (modeled on Germany's dual system): work 3+ days/week, school 2-3 days/week, 2021 cohort employment rate 94.9% (Workforce Development Agency). 2023 starting salaries: senior-high/vocational ~NT$28,000/month, university ~NT$33,000/month, graduate school ~NT$49,000/month; share starting at minimum wage: 58.3% senior-high/vocational, 23.9% university, 4.4% graduate school (Ministry of Labor 112-year new-hire wage statistics, via Global Views Monthly).

slides.1: Imagine telling your parents you want to skip university for a trade school. Many students never say it. Why does that idea feel so hard?
slides.2: SDG 4 wants good schools for everyone. That does not mean just one path. Taiwan's trade schools also teach real skills for real jobs.
slides.3: Taiwan's plants need many skilled workers. But fewer students pick that path now. In 2024, only 210,000 people learned a trade in school.
slides.4: The numbers are falling fast. Long ago, seven in ten students chose a technical school. Today, general high schools have far more students instead.
slides.5: There is an old label for these graduates: black hands. In other countries, the same worker is called a craftsman. Words like this matter.
slides.6: Even job-ready programs are not enough for some parents. They still want a college degree too. Without one, a teen can feel like an outsider.
slides.7: Now for some pride. At the 2024 WorldSkills contest in France, Taiwan sent 58 young competitors. They won 2 gold medals and ranked 4th among 69 countries.
slides.8: Taiwan then hosted the 2025 Asia skills contest in Taipei. The team won first place again there. That makes two wins in a row.
slides.9: There is also a training program based on Germany's system. Students work three days and study two days each week. Its graduates found jobs at a 94.9 percent rate.
slides.10: Instead of only sitting in classrooms, students could learn on the job too. This mixes real work with real study. Both sides gain something useful.
slides.11: Old workshops with old tools hurt study badly. Schools should buy new machines, not just new labs. Skills must match what factories use today.
slides.12: Middle school counselors could help too. Instead of naming university first, they could praise both paths equally. That kind of change could start early.
slides.13: Here is the real tension. If plants need skilled workers, fewer trade grads becomes a real danger. Even chip factories need trained workers, not only engineers.
slides.14: However, parents are not just stubborn. One new trade job in 2023 paid about NT$28,000 a month. One college job paid about NT$33,000.
slides.15: However, that pay gap hits new workers hardest. Over half of trade-school grads start at minimum wage. Only about a quarter of college grads do.
slides.16: However, a first paycheck is not a whole career. Skilled workers who win medals often earn much more later. A short-term gap can close over time.
slides.17: So here is where things stand. Fewer students choose technical schools each year. Yet these same schools keep winning medals and keep finding jobs.
slides.18: This matters even if you study something else today. Taiwan really needs both kinds of workers, because one path cannot succeed without the other.
slides.19: So question what you grew up believing about school. Ask why a degree feels safer than a skill. Then share a WorldSkills story with someone.
slides.20: Two paths built this whole island as one. Please respect both diplomas equally from today. Taiwan's future needs every skilled worker it can find.
